overview: Delegat Group is a New Zealand-headquartered, vertically integrated producer and global marketer of super-premium wine, best known for its flagship Oyster Bay brand (Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc and other varietals) and Barossa Valley Estate in South Australia. The Group owns and leases vineyards, operates wineries in Marlborough and Hawke's Bay (NZ) and the Barossa Valley (Australia), and sells directly into North America, the UK/Ireland/Europe, and Australia/NZ/Asia Pacific through its own in-market subsidiaries and distributor relationships. It is family-controlled, with founder and Chair Jim Delegat holding a majority stake (~66%), and trades on the NZX as a small-cap with limited free float.

business_model.summary: Delegat makes money by growing/sourcing grapes, crafting finished wine, and selling it globally under premium-positioned brands, capturing margin at every stage of the value chain rather than just bottling third-party fruit. Revenue is transactional (case sales to distributors/retailers each period, no subscription or contracted recurring revenue) but underpinned by durable, repeat-purchase consumer brand demand and multi-year distributor/retailer relationships. The business is highly working-capital intensive: wine inventory (grapes, bulk wine, bottled stock ageing through the pipeline) and biological work-in-progress (unharvested grapes carried at fair value under IAS 41/NZ IAS 41) together represented roughly NZ$200m+ of the ~NZ$1.14bn balance sheet at Dec-2025, funded substantially by ~NZ$307m of net debt. 'Super premium' positioning (retail price points generally above commodity/mid-market wine) supports gross margins in the high-40s percent and allows the Group to use price increases to offset volume softness, but it also means Delegat is more exposed than mass-market producers to discretionary consumer spending and premiumisation trends reversing.

revenue_streams.name: North America (USA and Canada)
revenue_streams.trend: recovering (H1 FY26 case volume still -8% but revenue/pricing improving as tariff impact eases)

revenue_streams.name: UK, Ireland and Europe
revenue_streams.trend: growing (H1 FY26 case volume +12% after two years of decline)

revenue_streams.name: Australia, NZ, China and Asia Pacific
revenue_streams.trend: growing (H1 FY26 case volume +16%; China +41% in FY25)

business_model.customer_type: B2B distribution to large retailers, wholesalers and distributors globally, ultimately consumed by premium-tier B2C wine drinkers; the Group also has in-house sales/marketing subsidiaries (Delegat USA, Delegat Europe, Delegat Australia) rather than relying purely on third-party distributors
business_model.geographic_mix: H1 FY2026 case-sales split: North America 43%, UK/Ireland/Europe 33%, Australia/NZ/China/Asia Pacific 24%. Production/asset base concentrated in Marlborough and Hawke's Bay, New Zealand, plus Barossa Valley, Australia (~NZ$46.6m of segment assets).

main_competitors: Villa Maria / Indevin (NZ Sauvignon Blanc peers)
Cloudy Bay (LVMH), Kim Crawford, Whitehaven, Nautilus and other Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc producers
E&J Gallo and other large diversified global wine groups
Numerous regional/private-label competitors engaging in price discounting in mature markets (UK, Australia)
competitive_position.market_position: Category leader in premium New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc; Oyster Bay ranks #1 premium Sauvignon Blanc in Australia, #2 premium Sauvignon Blanc in the USA by value, #1 premium Merlot in the UK, and #1 New Zealand wine brand in China by volume. Company targets the 'Super Premium' price tier specifically, distinct from both mass-market and ultra-luxury/cult wine segments.

moat_factors.description: Oyster Bay is a top-5 global white wine brand by value in several markets with genuine consumer pull, category-leading search interest, and >92 million consumer marketing reach; this supports price realisation even as volumes fluctuate.

Vertical integration into vineyards and NZ$768.7m of PP&E (owned land, vines, wineries) gives control over fruit quality/cost and insulates against grape price spikes that hit non-integrated bottlers, but it also means Delegat cannot flex supply down quickly when demand falls (fixed vineyard capacity).

New Zealand's (and Marlborough's) distinctive cool-climate Sauvignon Blanc style has an internationally recognised, hard-to-replicate terroir reputation that supports a price premium over generic Sauvignon Blanc.

Owned sales and marketing subsidiaries in the US, Europe and Australia (rather than pure third-party distribution) give closer retailer relationships and promotional control, called out by management as a competitive advantage.

Vertical integration from vineyard to bottle can produce a structural cost advantage versus smaller independent wineries, though large diversified competitors (Constellation, Treasury) have greater scale.

weaknesses: Wine is a low-switching-cost, highly competitive category — no lock-in for consumers or retailers, and shelf space/listings can be lost to a competitor's promotion in a single planning cycle
Single-varietal/single-brand concentration: Oyster Bay Sauvignon Blanc is disproportionately important to Group earnings, creating fashion/style risk if consumer tastes shift
Exposed to heavy competitor price discounting in mature markets (explicitly cited as the cause of FY2025 volume declines in UK/Ireland/Europe and Australia/NZ)
No long-term contracted revenue — case sales can swing materially half-to-half based on distributor/retailer inventory rebalancing, as seen in FY2025
US customer concentration: a single US customer represented ~10% or more of Group sales in both H1 FY2025 ($45.0m) and H1 FY2026 ($37.5m)

growth_drivers: Premiumisation and price realisation strategy: management has been implementing price increases across markets, delivering +2% revenue in FY2025 despite -12% case volumes

North America expansion: the US (>50 million premium wine consumers) is explicitly flagged as the Group's largest market and single biggest growth opportunity; management targets total case sales growth of 13% to 3.6 million by 2028

China and Asia Pacific: China case sales grew 41% in FY2025 with Oyster Bay now the #1 New Zealand wine brand there by volume; broadening distribution and digital engagement seen as a long-term growth lever
Brand extension beyond Sauvignon Blanc: Pinot Grigio is now a top-10 global premium varietal for Oyster Bay in the US; Group is investing in Pinot Gris, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir

Vineyard and winery capacity investment: >$250m invested in growth assets over the past four years (Hawke's Bay and Marlborough winery development, NZ vineyard developments), positioning supply for the medium-term sales plan, though capex is now tapering ($26.2m planned for FY2026 versus $59.9m in FY2025)
Large 2025 harvest (47,461 tonnes, +39% YoY) rebuilding inventory and supporting the FY2026 sales forecast of 3.3 million cases without supply constraint
White wine category tailwind: management and industry data point to white wine/lighter beverage occasions outperforming other wine categories, a style where NZ Sauvignon Blanc is well positioned

business.description: Management's own FY2025 commentary acknowledges consumers are 'drinking less,' with moderation driven by health, lifestyle and generational attitudes (particularly weaker among younger/Gen Z consumers) and premiumisation trend growth slowing as budgets tighten — a genuine secular headwind to category volume, not just a cyclical blip.

Explicitly cited as a cause of FY2025 case-sales declines in UK/Ireland/Europe (-15%) and Australia/NZ (-5%); in a maturing/shrinking category, competitors compete on price which pressures Delegat's premium positioning and/or volumes.
A single US customer accounted for 10%+ of Group sales in H1 FY2025 and H1 FY2026 (~$37-45m); loss or renegotiation of a top retail/distribution relationship would be material.

Oyster Bay Sauvignon Blanc dominates earnings; a shift in consumer taste away from Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc, or reputational damage to the Oyster Bay brand, would disproportionately hit the Group versus a diversified multi-brand competitor.

financial.description: Net debt of $307.0m at Dec-2025 (down from $328.6m at Jun-2025) against a $420m syndicated senior facility; H1 FY2026 interest expense was $8.9m against Operating EBIT of $50.7m — manageable but leaves limited headroom if EBITDA falls in a poor vintage/demand year, and ties the Group to bank covenant and refinancing risk.

Inventory ($143.1m) plus biological WIP ($61.2m) together exceeded $200m at Dec-2025; a demand downturn or further volume declines traps cash in unsold stock (as seen with FY2024's weak cash conversion), and wine inventory cannot be quickly liquidated without brand-damaging discounting.

Revenue is earned in USD, GBP, AUD and CAD but reported in NZD; the Group hedges with forward FX contracts and interest rate swaps, but mark-to-market swings on these derivatives create large, non-cash swings between 'Reported' and 'Operating' NPAT — e.g., a $17.8m fair-value derivative write-down inflated the H1 FY2025 Reported/Operating gap, versus only $6.2m in H1 FY2026. This creates reported-earnings volatility that can mislead if 'Reported NPAT' is used without reference to 'Operating NPAT'.

regulatory.description: The single largest identified risk. An April-2025 10% IEEPA tariff cut FY2025 Operating NPAT guidance from $55-60m to $47-50m and case-sales guidance by 5%. The tariff rate rose further to 15% by H1 FY2026 (a further ~NZ$2.5m adverse impact plus extra promotional investment). On 20 February 2026 the US Supreme Court ruled the IEEPA tariffs unlawful, and Delegat subsequently lifted FY2026 guidance to $60-62m NPAT partly on 'lower US tariffs on shipments from February.' However, the US administration replaced the struck-down tariffs: Section 122 tariffs were implemented as an interim measure, then from 24 July 2026 a new Section 301 'forced labour' tariff regime imposed an additional ~12.5% duty on New Zealand exports (stacking with the ~4.5% MFN wine tariff for an effective ~17% total on NZ wine into the US). This is a live, evolving risk — the Supreme Court win did not end tariff exposure, it merely reset the mechanism, and the FY2026 result (not yet reported as of Aug-2026) will be the first full read on the net impact of the Section 301 regime.

regulatory.risk: Alcohol regulation and health-driven policy trends
regulatory.description: Rising public-health and taxation scrutiny of alcohol in several developed markets (labelling, marketing restrictions, excise) could add cost or dampen category demand over time, compounding the consumption moderation trend.

macro.description: As a NZ IAS 41 biological-asset accounted business, grape fair-value swings directly hit reported earnings (e.g., FY2025's 39% larger harvest drove a $9.4m fair-value write-up versus a $5.0m write-down in the smaller FY2024 vintage) — climate variability (frost, drought, rain at harvest) in Marlborough and Hawke's Bay creates real earnings volatility outside management's control, and a run of poor vintages would both cut volumes and raise per-unit costs.

Super-premium wine is a discretionary purchase; a recession or sustained cost-of-living pressure in the Group's core developed markets (US, UK, Australia) would likely accelerate trade-down and volume declines beyond the already-observed moderation trend.

~$307m net debt is partly hedged via interest rate swaps, but a sustained higher-rate environment increases refinancing cost on the syndicated facility and reduces the value of a business whose asset base (vineyards, long-lived wine inventory) is capital- and duration-heavy.

execution.risk: Family control and small free float
execution.description: Chair Jim Delegat and family hold approximately 66% of shares on issue; minority shareholders have no practical influence over governance or capital allocation, and the resulting small free float (~34% of ~101m shares, spread across NZX retail/institutional holders) means thin trading liquidity, wide bid/ask spreads, and greater share-price sensitivity to any block trade or family sell-down. This is a persistent governance and liquidity risk, not a one-off event risk.
Long-tenured executive Chair (on the Board since the 2006 listing) and CEO Murray Annabell provide continuity, but succession planning risk exists in a founder/family-controlled structure.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global wine consumption is in gradual structural decline, particularly among younger/health-conscious consumers, with 'moderation' (drinking less but better) the dominant theme; white wine and lighter styles are forecast to outperform red/other categories, a relative tailwind for Delegat's Sauvignon Blanc-led portfolio. Premiumisation (trading up within the category) has slowed as consumers focus spend on necessities, but 'quality over quantity' behaviour still favours recognised premium brands like Oyster Bay over private label.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate-to-high — demand is discretionary and sensitive to consumer spending cycles, retailer/distributor destocking cycles (a major driver of the FY2025 volume decline), and is compounded by agricultural cyclicality (vintage yield/quality swings) on the supply side.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate — ~$307m net debt funds a capital- and inventory-intensive balance sheet; higher-for-longer rates raise financing costs and depress the present value of long-duration vineyard/winery assets.
key_input_costs: Grape/fruit costs (partially insulated by owned vineyards but still exposed via IAS 41 fair-value swings)
Ocean freight/logistics to US, UK and Asian markets
Marketing/promotional spend to defend shelf position against discounting competitors

recent_developments.event: Delegat cut FY2025 Operating NPAT guidance from $55-60m to $47-50m and case-sales guidance by 5% to 3,182,000, citing the new 10% US IEEPA tariff (effective April 2025) and resulting distributor uncertainty over Q4 FY2025 shipments.

FY2025 annual result: Operating NPAT $51.1m (-14%), Operating EBITDA $116.5m (-9%), global case sales 3,188,000 (-12%), broadly in line with the revised guidance. Reported NPAT rose 56% to $49.0m on favourable derivative/biological fair-value swings versus the prior year. Full-year dividend maintained at 20.0 cents per share fully imputed. FY2026 initial guidance: Operating NPAT $50-55m on 3.3 million case sales.

H1 FY2026 (six months to 31 Dec 2025) result: Operating NPAT $29.7m (+5%), Operating EBIT $50.7m (+5%), Operating EBITDA $65.6m (+6%), global case sales 1,688,000 (+3%) despite a further -8% decline in North America case volumes, offset by UK/Ireland/Europe +12% and Australia/NZ/Asia Pacific +16%. Net debt reduced to $307.0m (down $38.6m half-on-half). US tariff impact (now at 15%) plus incremental promotional spend cost approximately NZ$2.5m in the half. Board reaffirmed FY2026 Operating NPAT guidance of $50-55m.

US Supreme Court ruled the IEEPA-based tariffs (imposed since April 2025) unlawful. A subsequent balance-date subsequent event note in the H1 FY2026 interim report flags the Group 'continues to work through these uncertainties' as the US administration responded with alternative tariff mechanisms.

Delegat issued an upgraded FY2026 guidance announcement, lifting Operating NPAT guidance to $60-62 million (from $50-55m), citing stronger Q4 global case sales, lower US tariffs on shipments from February 2026, and favourable FX; global case sales guidance held at 3.3 million cases for the year.

A new Section 301 'forced-labour' tariff regime took effect, imposing an additional ~12.5% duty on New Zealand exports to the US (replacing the interim Section 122 mechanism), taking the effective total tariff on NZ wine into the US to roughly 17% (stacking with the ~4.5% MFN base rate) — meaning tariff cost has re-emerged in a different form even after the Supreme Court ruling, with the net FY2026/FY2027 impact not yet visible in a reported result.

FY2026 (year ended 30 June 2026) full-year results are due late August 2026 and had not been released as of this analysis date; the June-2026 guidance upgrade to $60-62m Operating NPAT is the most recent quantitative signal.

guidance.as_of: June 2026 guidance upgrade (post H1 FY2026 result of Feb-2026)

items.notes: Raised in June 2026 from the $50-55m range given at both the FY2025 result (Aug-2025) and reaffirmed at H1 FY2026 (Feb-2026); driven by stronger Q4 case sales, lower US tariffs on shipments from February 2026, and favourable FX. Original FY2025-set FY2026 guidance had itself already been cut once by the April-2025 tariff-driven guidance revision cycle affecting FY2025.

Held steady at 3.3 million (up from 3.2 million actual in FY2025) throughout FY2026 despite the tariff disruption; H1 FY2026 tracked at 1.688 million cases (+3% YoY), roughly half the full-year target.

items.target: Grow to 3.6 million cases by FY2028 (~13% growth over 3 years from FY2025's 3.2m)
items.notes: Interim milestones given as 3.3m (FY2026), 3.4m (FY2027), 3.6m (FY2028); North America is cited as the primary growth driver.

Down sharply from $59.9m in FY2025 and the >$250m invested over the prior four years; management guided to 'lower capital spending over the next three years, focusing mainly on replacing essential infrastructure and productivity initiatives' as major winery/vineyard growth projects complete.

items.target: 20.0 cents per share fully imputed (FY2025 actual)
items.notes: Directors maintained the payout at the prior year's level, citing 'underlying operational performance and continued strong cash flows'; FY2026 dividend not yet declared as of this analysis.

guidance.management_commentary: Chair Jim Delegat has repeatedly framed results against 'a challenging global market environment' shaped by US tariffs, supply-chain disruption and distributor/retailer inventory rebalancing, while emphasising the resilience of the brand portfolio and business model. CEO Murray Annabell's FY2025 commentary stressed 'decisive actions to align with evolving market conditions' (price increases, inventory management, leveraging distributor relationships to navigate tariffs) to protect long-term shareholder value. The June-2026 guidance upgrade release attributed the swing in fortunes explicitly to tariff relief and FX, signalling that management views the underlying demand/volume trend (steady at ~3.3m cases) as intact, with margin/profit volatility being driven predominantly by external trade-policy and currency factors rather than brand or category weakness.

bull_case: Tariff relief momentum: the February 2026 Supreme Court ruling and subsequent June 2026 guidance upgrade to $60-62m Operating NPAT (from $50-55m) show the FY2025-26 profit squeeze was substantially a trade-policy shock, not a demand collapse — case sales held at 3.3 million through the entire tariff disruption, and any further easing of the new Section 301 regime (via trade negotiation) would be a direct earnings tailwind

H1 FY2026 shows the operating recovery is broad and real: Operating NPAT +5%, EBIT +5%, EBITDA +6%, gross margin expanded to 49% from 48%, and net debt fell $38.6m half-on-half — evidence of price/mix discipline and cost control working even with North America volumes still down 8%

Balance-sheet and capital discipline: capex is tapering from $59.9m (FY2025) to $26.2m (FY2026) after a >$250m four-year investment cycle in Marlborough/Hawke's Bay wineries and NZ vineyards, freeing cash flow for debt reduction and/or dividend growth just as the new capacity comes fully online

Genuine brand moat in a structurally advantaged niche: Oyster Bay is a top-2-5 premium Sauvignon Blanc by value in the US, UK, Australia and Canada, and the #1 New Zealand wine brand in China (sales +41% in FY2025) — durable share leadership in the specific sub-category (white/lighter wine) forecast to outperform the broader declining wine category

UK/Ireland/Europe and Australia/NZ/APAC re-accelerating in H1 FY2026 (+12% and +16% case volumes respectively) after two years of decline driven by competitor discounting, suggesting Delegat has stabilised share outside its most tariff-exposed North American market
bear_case: Tariff risk is not resolved, only relabelled: the Supreme Court's IEEPA ruling has been followed by a new Section 301 'forced-labour' tariff (effective 24 July 2026) that takes the effective US duty on NZ wine to roughly 17% — worse than the original 10% IEEPA rate that first triggered the April-2025 guidance cut — and FY2026 results (due late Aug-2026) will be the first to show the real net impact; further escalation or a slow negotiated resolution could easily reverse the June-2026 guidance upgrade

Structural category decline: management's own commentary acknowledges wine consumption is falling, driven by health/moderation trends and weak Gen Z engagement — Delegat is fighting a shrinking pie in its core developed markets (North America case volumes have now fallen in five of the last six halves), and price increases used to offset volume losses have a ceiling before they simply accelerate share loss to discounting competitors

Single-brand, single-varietal concentration risk: Oyster Bay Sauvignon Blanc dominates Group earnings; any shift in consumer taste, reputational issue, or intensified private-label/discount competition in Sauvignon Blanc specifically would disproportionately impair the Group versus diversified multi-brand competitors like Constellation or Treasury Wine Estates

Governance and liquidity structure limits minority shareholder influence and share-price support: the Delegat family's ~66% holding leaves a thin free float, meaning low trading liquidity, wide spreads, and no realistic path to activist pressure, M&A premium, or index-driven demand — the stock's fate is tied to family capital-allocation preferences

Working-capital and balance-sheet strain in a downturn: with $307m net debt and $200m+ tied up in inventory/biological WIP, a renewed demand shock (further tariff escalation, recession, or a poor vintage) would simultaneously cut EBITDA and trap cash in unsold stock, as already seen in the weak FY2024 cash conversion, pressuring the dividend and covenant headroom

dcf_notes_for_analyst.summary: Delegat is family-controlled, thinly-traded, single-brand-concentrated, agriculturally cyclical and tariff-exposed. Consider a stacked WACC premium built from these structural factors, consistent with the approach used for other small-cap NZX family-controlled names in this project (e.g. ALF.NZ, CDI.NZ, AGL.NZ ~17-19% stacked WACC).

risk_premium_factors.factor: Small-cap NZX illiquidity / thin free float
risk_premium_factors.rationale: ~66% Delegat family ownership leaves only ~34% of ~101m shares as free float; thin daily trading volume typical of NZX small caps warrants a liquidity premium.
Majority family control with no realistic minority-shareholder influence over capital allocation, board composition or M&A; standard governance discount/premium applied to controlled companies.
Oyster Bay Sauvignon Blanc dominates Group earnings; lacks the multi-brand diversification of Constellation Brands or Treasury Wine Estates, raising idiosyncratic risk.

NZ IAS 41 biological-asset fair-value accounting creates real earnings volatility tied to vintage yield/quality; FY2024 vintage was materially weaker than FY2025 (+39% tonnage swing), directly moving margins and reported profit.

Live, unresolved risk — effective US tariff on NZ wine has moved from 0% (pre-Apr-2025) to 10% (IEEPA) to 15% (H1 FY26) and now ~17% (Section 301, effective 24-Jul-2026) despite a Supreme Court ruling against the original mechanism; North America is ~43% of case sales, making this a first-order, not tail, risk.

dcf_notes_for_analyst.suggested_total_premium_over_base_nzx_wa: +6% to +10.5% cumulative (stacked), reflecting a similarly-constructed WACC to the project's other family-controlled/small-float NZX agricultural names
cash_flow_base_year_caveats: FY2025 Operating NPAT ($51.1m) was tariff- and vintage-depressed; do not treat as peak or trough in isolation — it followed a -14% decline from FY2024's $59.7m and preceded a guided FY2026 recovery to $60-62m.

H1 FY2026 Reported NPAT ($22.8m) is NOT representative of run-rate; use Operating NPAT ($29.7m) which strips NZ IFRS fair-value swings on biological produce and derivatives — the Reported vs Operating gap has ranged from ~$2m to ~$28m across recent periods purely on non-cash FX/derivative mark-to-market and grape fair-value timing.
FY2026 full-year results (due late Aug-2026) are not yet published; the $60-62m guidance is management's own forecast, not an audited actual — flag this explicitly if used as the DCF base year.

Net debt of $307.0m at Dec-2025 should be used over the $328.6m Jun-2025 figure if a more current balance sheet date is preferred, noting the Group's debt is seasonal (peaks around harvest/vintage funding and unwinds through the selling season).
